title: AI Strategy and Business Value
objective: Connect business challenges, value hypotheses, feasibility, risks, KPIs, and ROI to prioritize AI initiatives and decide whether to scale or stop them.

sections.title: Making investment decisions from KPIs and the baseline
paragraphs: The business value of AI is defined not by “introducing AI,” but by how much it improves a specific business problem. For contact-center summarization assistance, measure agents’ after-call work time, repeat-contact rate, customer satisfaction, time required for quality checks, and operating costs as the preimplementation baseline.

Do not narrow the KPIs to a single metric. Even if processing time is reduced, increased misinformation or repeat contacts can worsen the customer experience and total costs. Record the value hypothesis, expected benefits, required investment, risks, measurement period, and responsible owner as one business case.

How to read the diagram: Move from `Baseline` to `Pilot`, and compare before and after implementation using consistently defined `KPI and ROI` measures. The endpoint of the arrow is not always `Scale`; the three evidence-based decisions are `Scale`, `Pause`, and `Stop`.

sections.title: Prioritize use cases by value, feasibility, and risk
paragraphs: When prioritizing AI candidates, do not rank them based solely on short-term revenue potential. Compare the scale of the business problem, value to the people affected, alignment with strategy, required data, ease of integration into business processes, operational capabilities, investment, and risks related to regulation, fairness, and trust using the same criteria.

Even when a candidate is expected to deliver high value, it should not be considered for immediate enterprise-wide deployment if the quality, permissions, or update status of the available data is unclear. Conversely, simply accumulating candidates that are easy to implement but have low strategic value will not produce results for the AI strategy. Separate the hypotheses to validate through pilots from the candidates that should begin only after their prerequisites have been established.

Prioritization decisions should not be confined to senior management; they should incorporate the perspectives of business owners, users, data owners, and risk, legal, and security stakeholders. Keep the basis for each score and the reasons for deferral so that the decisions can be revisited when their assumptions change.

sections.title: Monitor value and unintended impacts after implementation
paragraphs: Measuring the value of AI does not end when the pilot ends. As usage increases, input data, user behavior, business processes, operating costs, and impacts on customers may change. Continue measuring the KPIs defined before implementation and compare them with the baseline or a control group using the same criteria.

Monitoring should cover not only the expected benefits, but also errors, rework, exception handling, complaints, adverse impacts on specific users, and additional workload for staff. Even if usage increases, overall value may decline because of reduced quality or increased risk.

If outcomes fall short of expectations, investigate whether the cause lies in user training, business processes, data, the model, guardrails, or the scope of application. Decide whether to scale, pause temporarily for improvement, or terminate the initiative based on predefined evidence and accountable owners.

sources.label: Responsible AI: From Principles to Practice

checkpoints.prompt: A contact center leader is evaluating a pilot of an AI system that summarizes customer interactions. To create evidence from before and after implementation that can support the adoption decision, they must first define a baseline and comparable KPIs for the target operations. What is the most appropriate action to take before implementation?

choices.text: Use only the number of agents who use the AI as the success metric, without measuring operational data before implementation.
choices.explanation: Usage volume alone cannot show whether operational issues improved or how quality and cost changed.

choices.text: Measure after-call work time, repeat-contact rate, quality-review effort, customer satisfaction, and cost using the same definitions, and record the baseline.
choices.explanation: Even if after-contact work becomes shorter, repeat contacts, review effort, or costs may increase. Aligning metric definitions and baseline values before implementation makes it possible to compare the impact on staff and customers after implementation.

choices.text: Do not define the criteria for deciding whether the pilot succeeds, should be stopped, or needs improvement until the pilot ends.
choices.explanation: This would lead to decisions made for convenience after the fact, preventing evidence-based decision-making.

choices.text: If the AI output sounds natural, consider customer satisfaction and the repeat-contact rate unnecessary to measure.
choices.explanation: Natural-sounding text does not guarantee business value or customer impact, so the summary’s accuracy and usefulness must be evaluated separately.

checkpoints.prompt: At a retail company’s executive meeting, two AI candidates are being compared. Candidate A could significantly reduce work time, but the ownership, quality, and permitted use of the customer data have not been determined. Candidate B offers smaller benefits, but its data and business processes are ready. What is the most appropriate way to prioritize them?

choices.text: Compare them using the same criteria—value, feasibility, data and operational readiness, risk, and strategic fit—and treat candidate A as an initiative for establishing prerequisites or as a limited validation.
choices.explanation: Correct. This approach makes not only the potential value but also the implementation conditions and risks visible, allowing you to distinguish among piloting, deferring, and scaling based on evidence.

choices.text: Roll out candidate A company-wide based solely on the expected time savings, and resolve the data prerequisites after the rollout.
choices.explanation: Rolling it out while data ownership, quality, and permissions remain undetermined could undermine the feasibility of realizing its value and weaken governance.

choices.text: Adopt only candidate B permanently and do not document candidate A’s value hypothesis or unmet prerequisites.
choices.explanation: This would forfeit the opportunity to establish the prerequisites needed for a high-value candidate and would not constitute a strategic portfolio decision.

choices.text: Exclude data owners and frontline staff from the comparison and let the executive meeting make the decision alone.
choices.explanation: This makes it easier to overlook data-use conditions, integration into business operations, and actual risks.

checkpoints.prompt: After the insurance company expanded its contract-summary AI to all branches, the business leader confirmed that usage had increased, but so had the time staff spent making corrections and the number of correction requests from customers. What is the most appropriate response?

choices.text: Investigate correction time, correction requests, types of errors, affected branches, and business procedures, then decide whether to improve, temporarily suspend, or reduce the scope based on the causes.
choices.explanation: Correct. Continue measuring both the expected benefits and the undesirable effects, and use evidence to choose improvement or suspension as well as further expansion.

choices.text: Continue the rollout while ignoring the increased correction time and correction requests because usage has increased.
choices.explanation: Usage alone does not demonstrate value, and declining quality or customer impact could reduce the overall value.

choices.text: Prohibit staff from making corrections and send the AI-generated summaries directly to customers.
choices.explanation: This would amplify the impact of inaccurate summaries and eliminate human review and responsible operational oversight.

choices.text: Change the KPI definition so that usage alone appears to be the result.
choices.explanation: This would only conceal the problem and would not improve the original business issue or its impact on customers.
